L28: # Radau【19†#】
L29: 
L30: class scipy.integrate.Radau(fun, t0, y0, t_bound, max_step=inf, rtol=0.001, atol=1e-06, jac=None, jac_sparsity=None, vectorized=False, first_step=None, **extraneous)【20†[source]†github.com】【21†#】
L31: 
L32: 
L33: Implicit Runge-Kutta method of Radau IIA family of order 5.
L34: 
L35: The implementation follows 【22†[1]】. The error is controlled with a third-order accurate embedded formula. A cubic polynomial which satisfies the collocation conditions is used for the dense output.
L36: 
L37: Parameters:
L38: fun callable
L39: 
L40: 
L41: Right-hand side of the system: the time derivative of the state `y` at time `t`. The calling signature is `fun(t, y)`, where `t` is a scalar and `y` is an ndarray with `len(y) = len(y0)`. `fun` must return an array of the same shape as `y`. See vectorized for more information.
L42: 
L43: t0 float
L44: 
L45: 
L46: Initial time.
L47: 
L48: y0 array_like, shape (n,)
L49: 
L50: 
L51: Initial state.
L52: 
L53: t_bound float
L54: 
L55: 
L56: Boundary time - the integration won’t continue beyond it. It also determines the direction of the integration.
L57: first_step float or None, optional
L58: 
L59: 
L60: Initial step size. Default is `None` which means that the algorithm should choose.
L61: 
L62: max_step float, optional
L63: 
L64: 
L65: Maximum allowed step size. Default is np.inf, i.e., the step size is not bounded and determined solely by the solver.
L66: 
L67: rtol, atol float and array_like, optional
L68: Relative and absolute tolerances. The solver keeps the local error estimates less than `atol + rtol * abs(y)`. HHere rtol controls a relative accuracy (number of correct digits), while atol controls absolute accuracy (number of correct decimal places). To achieve the desired rtol, set atol to be smaller than the smallest value that can be expected from `rtol * abs(y)` so that rtol dominates the allowable error. If atol is larger than `rtol * abs(y)` the number of correct digits is not guaranteed.
L69: Conversely, to achieve the desired atol set rtol such that `rtol * abs(y)` is always smaller than atol. If components of y have different scales, it might be beneficial to set different atol values for different components by passing array_like with shape (n,) for atol. Default values are 1e-3 for rtol and 1e-6 for atol.
L70: jac{None, array_like, sparse_matrix, callable}, optional
L71: 
L72: 
L73: Jacobian matrix of the right-hand side of the system with respect to y, required by this method. The Jacobian matrix has shape (n, n) and its element (i, j) is equal to `d f_i / d y_j`. There are three ways to define the Jacobian:
L74: >   * If array_like or sparse_matrix, the Jacobian is assumed to be constant.
L75: >
L76: >   * If callable, the Jacobian is assumed to depend on both t and y; it will be called as `jac(t, y)` as necessary. For the ‘Radau’ and ‘BDF’ methods, the return value might be a sparse matrix.
L77: >
L78: >   * If None (default), the Jacobian will be approximated by finite differences.
L79: 
L80: It is generally recommended to provide the Jacobian rather than relying on a finite-difference approximation.
L81: jac_sparsity{None, array_like, sparse matrix}, optional
L82: 
L83: 
L84: Defines a sparsity structure of the Jacobian matrix for a finite-difference approximation. Its shape must be (n, n). This argument is ignored if jac is not None. If the Jacobian has only few non-zero elements in each row, providing the sparsity structure will greatly speed up the computations 【23†[2]】. A zero entry means that a corresponding element in the Jacobian is always zero. If None (default), the Jacobian is assumed to be dense.
L85: vectorized bool, optional
L86: 
L87: 
L88: Whether fun can be called in a vectorized fashion. Default is False.
L89: 
L90: If `vectorized` is False, fun will always be called with `y` of shape `(n,)`, where `n = len(y0)`.
L91: 
L92: If `vectorized` is True, fun may be called with `y` of shape `(n, k)`, where `k` is an integer. In this case, fun must behave such that `fun(t, y)[:, i] == fun(t, y[:, i])` (i.e. each column of the returned array is the time derivative of the state corresponding with a column of `y`).
L93: Setting `vectorized=True` allows for faster finite difference approximation of the Jacobian by this method, but may result in slower execution overall in some circumstances (e.g. small `len(y0)`).
L94:
